title: What Is a Computer, Really?
description: Peel back the abstractions and see how a computer actually works — from the CPU's fetch-decode-execute cycle to the OS juggling processes and threads.

segments.text: Welcome! Before we build distributed systems, we need to understand the machine itself. Think of a computer as a very fast, very obedient chef following recipes — one instruction at a time.
The CPU is that chef. It does three things on repeat: fetch an instruction from memory, decode what it means, then execute it. Fetch, decode, execute — billions of times per second.
Now the CPU needs ingredients close by. That's RAM — your working memory. It's blazingly fast but forgetful. The moment you cut the power, everything in RAM vanishes like a whiteboard being erased.

Disk storage is the pantry — much more space, but it takes longer to retrieve things. SSDs and hard drives keep your data safe even when the power goes out, but they're orders of magnitude slower than RAM.
Here's something to chew on. RAM can be a hundred thousand times faster than disk for random reads. That single fact shapes almost every design decision in systems engineering.
segments.thought_prompt: If RAM is so much faster, why don't we just use RAM for everything?

segments.text: Now, a process is a running program — your browser, your music player, each is a separate process. The OS gives each one its own private memory space, like giving each chef their own kitchen. They can't accidentally mess with each other's ingredients.

Threads are helpers within the same kitchen. A process can spin up multiple threads that share the same memory space. They work together, but sharing that space means they can bump into each other — which we'll explore deeply in a later module.

The operating system is the head chef — the manager. It decides which process gets CPU time, manages memory allocation, and handles I/O. Without the OS, every program would have to manage hardware directly. Chaos!

The OS uses context switching to give each process a turn on the CPU. It saves one process's state, loads another's, and the CPU resumes right where that process left off. This happens thousands of times per second.

Think about it — your computer feels like it's running dozens of programs simultaneously, but a single CPU core can only do one thing at a time. The OS creates the illusion of parallelism through rapid switching.
segments.thought_prompt: If context switching has overhead, what happens when you run too many processes at once?

segments.text: So here's our foundation: CPU executes instructions, RAM provides fast temporary storage, disk provides slow permanent storage, processes are isolated programs, threads share memory within a process, and the OS orchestrates everything. Every system we build sits on top of these primitives.
